brief: A low, carpet-level view shows a bubbling orange enamel fondue pot on a smoked-glass coffee table. Long forks with coloured tips rest in the pot, a cube of bread drips cheese, and a deep harvest-gold shag rug stretches toward wood panelling. The palette is avocado, burnt orange, mustard, chocolate brown and amber glass. Shag fibres are drawn as thousands of curling coloured-pencil strands. Marker gives the enamel and teak its smooth, saturated sheen. A tasselled lamp casts warm, smoky, slightly hazy light. The scene feels lived-in and nostalgic, with a fallen cocktail napkin and a cigarette-burned edge.

A broken slab of comb honey on a slate board is rendered in transparent watercolour glazes. Amber, raw sienna and burnt honey pool inside each wax cell, with glossy drips sliding off the edge. Around it, and seeping into the background, is a Vienna Secession mosaic. It is made of gold marker squares, small spiralling eyes and black-and-white chequer tiles, like a Klimt robe. The ornament is flat and the honey is fully three-dimensional and wet. The boundary between them is deliberate and crisp. Bees are absent; only one wing lies stuck in the comb. The mood is opulent, sticky and ceremonial.

A lost suede work glove, fingers curled, rests on the lip of a raw board-marked concrete stair. The view is a steep oblique from above. The whole sheet is built in compressed charcoal mass, dragged and smudged to imitate the timber grain cast into the concrete. Graphite pencil adds pinholes, aggregate pebbles and hairline cracks. The glove alone gets a warm tan wash of burnt umber against the slate and ash greys. The light is flat and overcast, with no cast shadow, only ambient occlusion pooling in the riser. The frame is cropped tight and heavy, almost oppressive, with the stair edge slicing diagonally across the composition.

An overhead view of a doorstep floor shows open tins of rangoli powder: vermilion, turmeric, parrot green, magenta and chalk white. Several tins are knocked over, and their contents fan out in soft cones and footprint-smudged drifts. The powder is built from dense layered spray, granular and matte, piled so that tiny ridges cast miniature shadows. A half-finished symmetric pattern begins at one corner, its lines wobbling where fingers released the grains. The tin rims are pen-crisp, dented and lettered. Warm late-morning light rakes from one side. The image is busy, festive and joyfully accidental.

An antique cast-iron sewing machine is shown three-quarter view, painted entirely in Prussian blue watercolour on heavy cotton rag. Highlights are reserved paper white, like a sun print, and the image appears tonally inverted in feel: the darkest blue sits where light would fall hardest. The decals on the arm, the balance wheel and the thread spool are rendered with obsessive accuracy, but every edge has the soft bleed of chemistry rather than a lens. A length of fabric trails off the bed and out of frame. Faint brush-coated streaks at the margins reveal the hand-applied emulsion. The image is quiet, archival and cool.

A cracked CD jewel case lies on a pale terrazzo floor, the disc half slid out. Its mirrored face throws razor-thin rainbow diffraction arcs in lilac, seafoam and Miami pink. The ground is a soft airbrushed spray gradient running from dusty magenta to cyan, grainless and synthetic. Every scuff and hairline fracture in the clear plastic is drawn in fine technical pen, catching hard white glints. The case floats slightly off-centre and low in the frame, under an empty pastel sky that dissolves toward the top edge. The light is cold showroom fluorescence. The mood is nostalgic, glossy and faintly lonely, a mall at closing time.

A tall stack of vinyl records is seen edge-on and slightly from above. The top record sits askew, exposing its grooved face. Everything is ink only: pure black pen on bone-white paper. The microgrooves are drawn as dense concentric hairlines whose spacing tightens and loosens until the surface physically shimmers and moirés like Bridget Riley. The paper label is left blank cream with a crisp spindle hole. Reflected light along the groove ridges appears as a broad radial band where the lines thin to nothing. There is no colour and no grey wash, only line density making form. The image is hypnotic, vibrating and meticulous.

The view looks through a pawnshop window at a single gold signet ring on burgundy velvet. Across the foreground glass runs mirror-reversed gilded lettering with drop shadows in cobalt and black outline, slightly out of focus. Through it, the ring is razor sharp: scratches on the bezel, a worn engraved crest, velvet pile. Metal surfaces come from layered ochre, raw sienna and warm white marker over burnished pen contours, imitating gold leaf's hot specular flash. A faint reflection of a street and a passer-by ghosts across the glass. The mood is intimate and a little melancholy, commerce and heirloom overlapping.

The interior of a tractor cab looks through a dusty windshield at a ploughed field. In the foreground, a dented green thermos cup steams on the dashboard beside a work-worn hand. The whole image carries the grain of documentary film: a fine spray stipple layered over every surface. The colour is faded and warm, with olive, mustard, faded denim and sun-tired red, and the shadows lift toward milky brown. Coloured pencil gives the steering wheel cracks and the knuckle creases. A soft vignette closes the corners, and a single hair-like scratch runs vertically through the frame. The image feels candid, overheard and unposed.

A rusted black roadster bicycle leans against a freshly painted homestead wall. The wall is flat, bold Ndebele geometry: stepped chevrons in ultramarine, egg-yolk yellow, emerald and rose, all outlined in thick black bands. The wall is rendered in flat marker fields with hard edges. The bicycle is hyperreal in pen and pencil: chain grease, perished rubber, a frayed rope tying a sack to the rack. The midday sun throws a crisp, distorted spoke shadow across the painted patterns, bending over their geometry. The composition is frontal and architectural, celebrating a confident clash of handmade order and a used object.

A glistening savoury aspic, unmoulded onto a cut-glass platter, is studded with halved quail eggs, parsley sprigs and coins of carrot. It is painted in many thin watercolour glazes of pale amber and celadon. Everything inside is seen through the trembling gel, refracted and slightly magnified. Specular highlights sit as razor-white reserved shapes along the ribbed curves. The platter's facets throw small prismatic sparks onto a starched tablecloth. Shadows are coloured and transparent, tinted gold where light passes through the jelly. The image is retro, uncanny and almost too glossy to trust.

A freshly racked triangle of billiard balls sits on deep viridian baize, seen from low and close. Each ball's lacquer reflects its neighbours. Through layered coloured pencil burnished to a high gloss, those reflections become Delaunay-like rings of simultaneous contrast. Orange edges vibrate against ultramarine, and violet halos sit against lemon. The numbered white discs are perfect, with slight print misregistration. The overhead lamp produces a single hard white star on every sphere, repeated like a chorus. The felt nap is drawn as fine directional strokes. The image is rhythmic, chromatic and spinning even while perfectly still.

Two clenched fists bound in boxing hand wraps are shown close and frontal. The reserved terracotta orange of fired clay forms the skin and cloth, set against a glossy lustrous black slip ground. The anatomy is photographically exact: veins, split knuckles, frayed tape fibres, sweat beads. That detail is drawn in fine raised black relief lines and diluted golden-brown wash, the way vase painters drew musculature. A meander border frames the bottom edge. There are only two colours plus thinned washes. The ground shows the subtle radial sheen of a curved pot surface. The image is athletic, ancient and immediate.

A raw ribeye on creased pink butcher paper is rendered with obsessive marbling, gloss and fibrous grain. Horizontal bands of the image are torn and displaced sideways, as if the file corrupted mid-render. Within those slices, the red, green and blue channels separate into offset marker layers of crimson, acid cyan and lime. Some strips repeat the same sliver of fat three or four times. Others smear into long pixel-dragged streaks of flat colour. Untouched areas stay utterly photographic. The tension comes from appetite interrupted by error, and the composition is a centred slab cut by violent horizontals.

Prickly pear pads heavy with ripe tunas are painted onto dark amate bark. Build the ground from dense fibrous flow-field strokes in tobacco brown and charcoal, with the pounded lattice of the bark showing through. Paint the cactus in opaque, saturated pigments of vermilion, magenta and chartreuse, as in Otomi bark painting, but with hyperreal volume: glochid tufts as minute pale pen dots, waxy bloom on the fruit, one tuna split open to wet seeded pulp. Fine white contour flicks frame each form against the dark bark. The background stays raw.

A halved jackfruit rests on plain unprinted mill paper in the manner of a Kalighat pat. Give it a bold, fluid sepia outline that swells and thins in single confident sweeps, then fill it with transparent watercolour shading that rolls the volume hard toward the outline. The interior is hyperreal: golden saffron arils, sticky latex threads, pale fibrous rags and the knobbly green-ochre rind. Scatter tin-silver highlight flecks across the wet arils. Leave no background, only the paper's soft wear, so the sweeping outline contrasts with the obsessive detail of the fruit's inner fibres.

Fill the sheet with even Prussian-cyan spray with a faint chemical mottle, like a diazo blueprint. Over it, draw a trumpet's valve cluster and lead pipe in white gel pen and fine white pencil only. Dimension ticks, centre lines and leader arrows frame the drawing in the margins, but the instrument itself is rendered hyperreally. Valve-cap knurling, finger-buttons, solder seams and warped reflections of the room curving across the brass are all expressed through white hatching density alone. The highlights are the bare brightest white, and the shadows are left as untouched blue. The drawing is cool, technical and bright on both sides of the sheet.

A heap of guineafowl feathers sits on raw cotton, and the feathers' white-spotted charcoal plumage echoes bògòlanfini resist dots. Lay the ground in coarse woven ochre and fermented-mud brown, divided into loose hand-ruled panels of chevrons, crosses and dot rows in thick dark earth pigment. The feathers are rendered hyperreally over the top in charcoal mass and soft graphite: each barb, each pearl-white spot catching light, the iridescent blue-grey quill bases. Matte earth tones dominate. The only sheen is on the rachis. The feathers spill across panel borders.

A wet silicone swim cap and a coiled lane rope sit on pool-deck tiles. The composition is constrained like Otl Aicher's pictogram system: only horizontals, verticals and forty-five-degree diagonals, and a palette locked to signal green, pool blue, safety orange, silver and white. Lay each colour field in clean marker. Inside those fields, render hyperreal detail: water droplets beading on the cap, stretched creases, the moulded float discs of the lane rope, grout lines filled with chlorine scale. Edges between colours stay crisp and graphic, so it reads as a sign from afar and a photograph up close.

A massive barnacled anchor chain descends diagonally into turquoise depth while slanted shafts of noon light fan down from the surface. Build the water in stacked watercolour glazes, from teal and viridian near the top to deep Payne's grey below. Lift the light shafts out with long soft chalky pastel streaks and fine spray for suspended particles. The chain is fully hyperreal: rust scale, sea-squirts, kelp threads swaying, and caustic light patterns rippling across each link. The links fade bluer with distance, and the image feels calm, cold and heavy.
